headline: Hanashi is Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *panas-.
Furui is derived from the verb 旧る (furu, “to age”) plus し (-shi), an adjective-forming suffix.
Hazukashii went padukasiki → ɸadukaɕiki → ɸadukaɕiː → ɸad͡zukaɕiː → hazukaɕii.
Kesshite is from the conjunctive form of the verb 決する (kessuru, “to decide”).
Hikōjō is 飛行 (hikō, “aviation”) plus 場 (-jō, “place”).
Taisetsu is 大 (tai, “of great intensity”) plus 切 (setsu, “urgent, pressing, close”).
Mainen is 毎 (mai-, “every”) plus 年 (nen, “year”).
Igaku is first attested in Japanese in the late 1400s, in the Bunmei Hon Setsuyō-shū dictionary.
Kamu is cognate with Okinawan 食む (kamun, “to eat”), and a doublet of 醸む (kamu, “to brew”).
Koe went kowe → koe from Proto-Japonic *kəwai, and its further derivation is unknown.
Nanoka was nanuka in the Man'yōshū of circa 759, and the nanoka reading is first cited from the late Edo period.
Kuru comes from Old Japanese 來 (ku), and the source compares する (suru), from Old Japanese す.
Kissaten is 喫茶 (kissa, “drinking tea”) plus 店 (-ten, “shop; store”).
Mado may be 目 (ma, “eye”) plus 門 (to, “gate, opening”): an opening for looking through.
Nishi may originally be 去に (ini, “going away”) plus し (shi, “wind; (by extension) direction”).
Amari is the stem form of the verb 余る (amaru), appearing in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Bijutsukan is 美術 (bijutsu, “art”) plus 館 (kan, “public building”).
Hikaru's initial hika- is related to ぴかぴか (pikapika, “glitteringly, sparklingly”).
Satō is an orthographic borrowing from Chinese 砂糖 (shātáng).
To may be related to the only certainly attested Kara word, 梁, meaning “gate, door”, per Beckwith (2004).
Yaku appears in the Kojiki of 712 CE, from Proto-Japonic *yak-.
Ike is Old Japanese, first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE, from Proto-Japonic *ikay.
Gijutsu is first attested in Japanese in 1563, and was later repurposed as a calque of English mechanical art.
Kibishii was kibishi, “tight, close, without gaps”, first cited to roughly 830.
Obasan is a compound of 伯母 (oba) plus さん (san).
Shokuryōhin is 食料 (shokuryō) plus 品 (-hin).
Otōto was otopito, from 弟 (oto, “younger sibling”) plus 人 (hito, “person”).
Chikaku is the noun use of the stem of classical 近し (chikashi, “near”), equivalent to modern 近い.
Chiisai went */tipisasi/ → /tiɸisasi/ → /t͡ɕiwisaɕi/ → /t͡ɕiːsaɕi/ → /t͡ɕiːsai/, and its derivation is uncertain.
Muzukashii is related to 憤る (muzukaru) and 憤る (mutsukaru).
